newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. envoy says New York police can be overzealous.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says New York police can be overzealous.

text.p: Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said hostility toward foreign diplomats was increasing and New York police could be overzealous in issuing parking fines.

In a speech to the Association for a Better New York, Richardson said there was an "alarming upswing in angry confrontations, verbal abuse and an atmosphere of growing hostility toward diplomats and their families."
He said he thought both sides had reasonable arguments to back up their case as well as "examples of unfortunate behaviour by the other."

"Double parking or blocking a fire hydrant threatens the health and safety of every New Yorker," he said. "Diplomatic immunity does not grant one a license to simply disregard the law or fail to pay their parking tickets."

But he said diplomats had "a right to be shielded from overzealous and unfair ticketing of their vehicles," adding that one could not expect U.S. envoys abroad to be treated fairly if "we are not doing the same here in America."

At issue is proposed parking regulations for the 185 foreign embassies, called missions, accredited to the United Nations. New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani wanted to remove special license plates of diplomats who routinely ignored parking tickets and other violations.

But after the U.N. legal counsel said parts of Giuliani's plan, at first endorsed by Richardson, violated international law, the State Department came up with an alternative that is still in limbo. The State Department issues the plates.
The alternative would deny the foreign missions a plate the next time they applied for one. This would punish the mission but not necessarily the same diplomat who received the tickets.

The battle over the parking rules has angered New York residents, who see diplomats flout regulations, and has created a debate among some U.N. envoys that had escalated into a public relations disaster for the world body.
Giuliani earlier this year suggested that the United Nations could leave town and the waterfront site could be reclaimed for city buildings.
